statement: In people who drink alcohol, mostly people with heavy drinking who had just stopped drinking in detoxification centres, a short course of paracetamol (acetaminophen) at usual doses compared with placebo does not detectably raise the liver enzyme ALT at an early measurement in five randomized trials of 901 people (pooled difference about 0.1 units per litre, 95% CI about −1.3 to 1.5, editors' recalculation; the paper prints a standardized difference as if it were in units per litre), and no trial reported liver failure or death; three trials that measured later found modest ALT rises with longer use, mostly just after stopping, which had gone in the one trial that checked (Rumack et al., 2012). No trial tested paracetamol taken for a hangover after a single night of heavy drinking; no events among 551 treated people cannot rule out rare serious liver injury (upper 95% limit about 5 in 1,000, editors' calculation); and the review was funded by a paracetamol maker, which reviewed the manuscript, the authors' employer had contracts with paracetamol makers, its authors wrote all five pooled trials, and it did not assess the trials' risk of bias. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In trials with people who drink, mostly heavy drinkers who had just stopped, a short course of paracetamol at usual doses did not raise a liver blood test compared with a dummy pill, and nobody had liver failure. Small rises appeared in some trials when people took it for longer. No trial looked at paracetamol for a hangover after one night of drinking, and the review was paid for by a paracetamol maker whose researchers ran the trials.
population: People who drink alcohol in five randomized trials (551 on paracetamol, 350 on placebo): mostly people with heavy drinking who had just stopped drinking in detoxification centres (four trials) and moderate drinkers who kept drinking (one trial)
exposure: A short course of paracetamol (acetaminophen) at usual doses (doses and durations are on the study card)
outcome: Change in serum ALT from baseline at an early measurement; ALT at later measurements; liver dysfunction, liver failure and death
magnitude: Pooled difference in mean change in ALT (paracetamol minus placebo): printed as 0.0 (95% CI −0.2 to 0.1) and labelled IU/L, which matches a standardized difference (editors' recalculation −0.04, 95% CI −0.17 to 0.10); in IU/L about 0.1 (95% CI −1.3 to 1.5; editors' calculation). Later, unpooled: ALT higher with paracetamol by 12.6 and 8.4 IU/L in two trials just after the end of a course, and by 18.7 IU/L (8.1 at the lower dose) in a third, gone at that trial's last measurement. Liver dysfunction, failure or death: none reported (upper 95% limit about 0.5% for 551 treated people; editors' calculation).

evidence.extracted: Five trials (551 on acetaminophen, 350 on placebo) were pooled with a fixed-effect model: the difference in mean change in ALT is printed as 0.0 IU/L (-0.2 to 0.1; labelled '97% CI' in the Results and '95%CI' in the Abstract), Q = 1.7, I2 = 0. Recalculated from Table 1, these figures are a standardized difference (-0.04, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.10), as the forest-plot legend says; in IU/L the pooled difference is 0.09 (95% CI -1.27 to 1.46) (editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Results, 1st, 5th and 7th paragraphs; Abstract › Main Results
evidence.extracted: No randomized trial, included or excluded, reported liver dysfunction, liver failure or death; AST, INR, bilirubin and glutathione S-transferase changes were similar between groups where reported, apart from a rise in INR in people taking warfarin.

At later, unpooled measurements ALT was higher with acetaminophen than placebo by 12.6 IU/L (Dart 2010) and 8.4 IU/L (Heard 2007, statistically significant), mostly just after the end of dosing, and by 18.7 and 8.1 IU/L at the higher and lower dose in a trial of people taking warfarin (Parra 2007; Table 2's means give 18.3 for the higher dose), with no difference at that trial's last measurement.

Four of the six included trials (four of the five pooled) enrolled people with heavy drinking admitted to detoxification, who started acetaminophen soon after their last drink and had no alcohol during the trial; one enrolled moderate drinkers who kept drinking. In two pooled trials dosing had ended before the pooled measurement.

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Footnotes › Financial disclosure; References 6 to 10
evidence.extracted: The protocol was not registered and no assessment of bias in the trials was done. The review was funded by an investigator-initiated grant from McNeil Consumer Healthcare to Denver Health; the sponsors are stated to have had no role in design, performance, analysis or authorship, but the sponsor reviewed the final manuscript. Five authors are Denver Health employees, and Denver Health has contracts with McNeil and Cadence (acetaminophen makers) and Cumberland (IV acetylcysteine maker); one author consulted for McNeil on behalf of Denver Health and testified for McNeil in 2010 litigation; review authors are authors of all five pooled trials.

risk_of_bias.note: Randomized trials with an objective laboratory outcome, but the review assessed no risk of bias, searched published trials only, and is of critically low confidence; the trials share authors and partly a funder with the review.

indirectness.note: Mostly recently abstinent people in detoxification, ALT as a surrogate at one early measurement; not paracetamol taken for a hangover after a single night of heavy drinking.

imprecision.note: The interval for the ALT difference (about −1.3 to 1.5 IU/L) excludes clinically meaningful rises; rare serious injury is not addressed by this outcome, as the claim states.

publication_bias.note: Not downgraded: no sign of missing trials, but only published trials from largely one group were sought, and a five-trial funnel plot cannot show much.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness, giving low. 'Does not detectably change' is used for the early ALT measurement because the recalculated interval excludes meaningful rises; the claim does not extend this to rare serious liver injury, to longer use, or to use during a hangover. Status replicated by the same team: the five pooled trials agree but share investigators with each other and with the review. Placed in section 6 with the other interaction claims; it answers the day-after question about the safety of a common hangover medicine.
